lec05kp11-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp11-u01-p1-title.text: Weight-0.2 A costs 2 to delete but weight-1 B only 0.01: cost depends on curvature, not size

lec05kp11-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p1-bridge.text: Network size can be tuned (KP10). How much does deleting one connection of a trained network cost?

lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p1|Two local quadratic loss curves: A weight 0.2, curvature 100, deletion cost 2; B weight 1, curvature 0.02, deletion cost 0.01.

lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-151.name: term:Pruning
lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-151.text:
Pruning: remove some connections or
units so the model has fewer
adjustable parts; check performance
after deleting.

lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-152.name: term:Curvature
lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-152.text:
Curvature: how fast the slope of the
loss changes, measured by the second
derivative; with large curvature a
small step changes the cost a lot.

lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-153.name: term:Hessian
lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-153.text:
Hessian: the matrix H of all second
partial derivatives; H\_ii is the
curvature along direction i.

lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-155.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p1#155
lec05kp11-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp11-p1-155.text: Small-weight A costs 200 times as much to delete as B: changing a little does not mean affecting little.

lec05kp11-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp11-u01-p2-title.text: Substituting δw = −w gives saliency s = ½Hw²: A is 2, B is 0.01, a 200-fold gap

lec05kp11-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p2-bridge.text: Deletion cost depends on curvature, not weight size: A costs 2 and B only 0.01. Can slope and curvature estimate that cost before deleting?

lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p2|Four-step derivation of saliency and, on a log scale, A at 2 and B at 0.01, a 200-fold gap.

lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-18.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p2#18
lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-18.text: Saliency of A and B (log scale)

lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-36.name: term:Saliency
lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-36.text:
Saliency sᵢ: an estimate of how much the cost rises
when weight i is deleted; an approximation, not a
measured loss.

lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-38.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p2#38
lec05kp11-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp11-p2-38.text: A: ½ × 100 × 0.2² = 2; B: ½ × 0.02 × 1² = 0.01. The larger-weight B is deleted first.

lec05kp11-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp11-u01-p3-title.text: Saliency is only an estimate: delete in small steps, retrain, validate and re-estimate

lec05kp11-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p3-bridge.text: Substituting δw = −w gives saliency s = ½Hw²: A is 2, B is 0.01, a 200-fold gap. When does the estimate fail, and how does it fit a pruning loop?

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3|The four-step pruning loop (train, estimate saliency, delete a few, retrain and check, back to step 2) and four cases where the estimate fails.

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-4.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3#4
lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-4.text: A checkable pruning procedure: a four-step loop

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-22.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3#22
lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-22.text:
Retrain and check
on validation data

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-27.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3#27
lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-27.text:
Back to step 2: re-estimate after every batch; never treat
one ranking as permanent truth

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-29.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3#29
lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-29.text: Saliency is only an estimate: it fails in these four cases

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-32.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3#32
lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-32.text:
The first-order term g need
not be small, so it cannot be
dropped.

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-35.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p3#35
lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-35.text:
Higher-order terms may no
longer be negligible.

Weights may be coupled, so the

A negative value must not be
read as "safe".

lec05kp11-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp11-p3-43.text: So: delete in small steps, re-measure the cost, retrain the rest and keep the best validation model.

lec05kp11-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp11-u01-p4-title.text: With a weight penalty, α = 0.1 picks B (0.30 < 0.50); α = 0 looks only at data error and picks A

lec05kp11-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p4-bridge.text: Saliency is only an estimate, so we delete in small steps, retrain and re-estimate. If we instead change the objective to prefer small weights, how is the total cost written?

lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p4|Stacked bars: at α = 0.1 model A totals 0.50 and B 0.30, so B; at α = 0 A is 0.10 and B 0.20, so A.

lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-5.name: term:Regularization
lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-5.text:
Regularization: add a restriction or preference on the model beyond the
data error; P is the weight penalty and α ≥ 0 sets its share. α depends on
the error scale (sum or mean), so do not copy it across setups.

lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-7.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p4#7
lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-7.text: α = 0.1: total cost = data error + α × penalty

lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-24.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p4#24
lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-24.text:
blue: data error; orange:
α × penalty

lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-26.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p4#26
lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-26.text: α = 0: total cost = data error + α × penalty

lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-41.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p4#41
lec05kp11-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp11-p4-41.text: Choose α on validation data; a smaller total cost does not guarantee a smaller test error.

lec05kp11-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp11-u01-p5-title.text: Saturating penalty: 0.0385, 0.5, 0.9 at w = 0.2, 1, 3; zero slope at 0 does not force exact zeros

lec05kp11-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p5-bridge.text: With a weight penalty, α = 0.1 picks B. What shape should the penalty P take so large weights are not punished too much?

lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p5|Saturating penalty and derivative curves; ρ is 0.0385, 0.5, 0.9 at w = 0.2, 1, 3, and the derivative is zero at the origin.

lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-4.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p5#4
lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-4.text: The saturating penalty ρ and its derivative (horizontal axis: weight w, τ = 1)

lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-182.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p5#182
lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-182.text: w = 0.2, 1, 3: ρ ≈ 0.0385, 0.5, 0.9; large weights saturate at 1. (computed)

lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-187.name: term:Saturating penalty
lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-187.text:
Saturating penalty: τ > 0 is the scale; for very
large weights the penalty approaches 1, called
saturation. Compare scales with absolute values:
|w| ≪ τ means near zero.

lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-188.name: term:Weight elimination

lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-190.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p5#190
lec05kp11-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp11-p5-190.text: The derivative is zero at w = 0: finite updates do not guarantee exactly zero, so a threshold ε does the deleting.

lec05kp11-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp11-u01-p6-title.text: Deleting connections, deleting units and shrinking values differ; doubling A makes the term 8 times

lec05kp11-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p6-bridge.text: The saturating penalty has zero slope at 0, so weights need not become zero. Is one connection enough, and how do unit outputs and weight norms affect complexity?

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p6|Three columns comparing deleting connections, deleting units and shrinking values, and bars showing the source's complexity term growing 8 times when A doubles.

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-8.text:
Check: performance on the
data after deleting.

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-12.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p6#12
lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-12.text:
Remove the whole unit

Check: whether the next
layer lost this signal path.

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-18.text:
Weights or unit outputs
get smaller; connections
and units remain. The

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-20.name: fig:lec05-kp11-p6#20
lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-20.text:
Check: a small output can

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-24.text:
A: a common bound on each unit's
sum of absolute weights; d: input
dimension; N: sample size.

lec05kp11-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp11-p6-31.text: Fix d, N; double A: 2³ = 8 times

lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-21.name: term:Residual
lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-21.text:
Residual: the true target minus the current
prediction, eₙ = tₙ − ŷₙ, n is the sample index.

lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-22.name: term:Cascade correlation
lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-22.text:
Cascade correlation: add one hidden unit at a time
that responds to the current residual, then
retrain the output; the new unit receives the
inputs and earlier hidden units.

lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-24.text: Teaching score S (single output): candidate output v against residual e

lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-26.text:

lec05kp11-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp11-p7-36.text: With e = (−1, 1): pick the candidate with the largest S, freeze its input weights, then retrain the output.

Check: the penalty is part of the objective; only zeroing or
removing deletes.

steps.label: Pruning, regularization and simulations
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp11 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 11 pages; every number is computed by program. The scatter on page 8 is redrawn from the source's setup with the fixed seed 20261025 and is not the source's original sample; 480 to 25, the momentum parameters and the boundary change are the source's report and were not rerun.

steps.label: Deletion cost and curvature
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP11. The prerequisites are cost and gradient (KP06), second derivatives and curvature, the Taylor expansion and validation data (KP10). Pruning removes some connections or units so the model has fewer adjustable parts; the goal is not to delete the most but to reach a simpler model at an acceptable loss. To set a weight to zero, the change δw equals minus w. On the left, A has weight 0.2 but a steep curve, curvature H equal to 100, so the deletion cost is one half times 100 times 0.2 squared, equal to 2. In the middle, B has weight 1 but a flat curve, curvature only 0.02, and the cost is one half times 0.02 times 1 squared, equal to 0.01 (computed by program). So the small-weight A costs 200 times as much to delete as B. Curvature is how fast the slope of the loss changes, measured by the second derivative; the Hessian arranges all second partial derivatives in a matrix, and H_ii is the curvature along direction i. Do not treat changing only a little as affecting only a little. Next, the next page covers the derivation of saliency.

steps.label: Saliency derivation
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on deletion cost and curvature. This page derives saliency in four steps. Step one, the change in cost is approximated by the Taylor expansion: ΔJ is about the sum of g_i times δw_i plus one half the sum of H_ij δw_i δw_j. Step two, near a minimum the slope g is about zero and the first term vanishes. Step three, the diagonal approximation drops the cross terms between different weights, leaving one half the sum of H_ii times δw_i squared. Step four, substitute δw_i equal to minus w_i and define the saliency s_i as one half H_ii w_i squared; it estimates the deletion cost and is an approximation, not a measured loss. On the right, on a log scale: A is 2 and B is 0.01, and 2 over 0.01 is 200 times, so by this local estimate B is deleted first even though its weight is larger (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the pruning procedure and the conditions of the estimate.

steps.label: Pruning procedure
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the derivation of saliency. Saliency is not a measured value after deletion, so the procedure must include re-evaluation and retraining, and one ranking must not be treated as permanent truth. The top is a four-step loop: train to a good point, estimate each connection's saliency, delete a few low-saliency connections, retrain and check on validation data, then return to step two. Stop by validation performance, an allowed loss increase or a resource budget; the smaller network after deleting is not guaranteed to be more accurate each time. Below are four cases where the estimate fails: not yet near a minimum the first-order term need not be small; when deleting too much the higher-order terms matter; deleting several weights at once may couple them; and with negative curvature in the Hessian a negative value must not be read as safe. Methods with the full Hessian can also account for how other weights compensate, at the price of more storage and computation. Next, the next page covers regularization.

steps.label: Regularization
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the pruning procedure. Pruning changes the structure, while regularization first changes the objective: the total cost equals the data error plus α times the weight penalty P. α is at least zero and sets the relative weight; if the data error is a sum or a mean the scale differs and the same α acts differently, so it cannot be copied across setups. The example takes α equal to 0.1: model A has data error 0.10 and penalty 4, total 0.10 plus 0.1 times 4 equal to 0.50; model B has data error 0.20 and penalty 1, total 0.20 plus 0.1 times 1 equal to 0.30, so B is chosen. With α equal to 0 only the data error counts, and A is chosen because 0.10 is below 0.20 (computed by program). α should be chosen on validation data; a smaller total cost does not mean the test error is necessarily smaller. Next, the next page covers the saturating penalty.

steps.label: Saturating penalty
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on regularization. The saturating penalty is ρ(w) equal to w squared over τ squared plus w squared, where τ above zero is the scale; for very large weights the penalty approaches 1, called saturation. The total penalty P is the sum of ρ over the weights. With τ equal to 1, at w equal to 0.2, 1 and 3, ρ is about 0.0385, 0.5 and 0.9 (computed by program). Compare scales with absolute values: |w| much smaller than τ means near zero. The derivative ρ prime equals 2 τ squared w over the square of τ squared plus w squared; at w equal to 0 it is 0, so finite updates do not guarantee exactly zero. Weight elimination encourages shrinking during training and then periodically zeroes or deletes weights with |w_i| below ε; ε is the deletion threshold and τ the penalty scale, with different roles. Next, the next page covers the three operations and the norm.

steps.label: Operations and norm
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the saturating penalty. A connection is not a whole unit, and a unit is not a whole signal path. Deleting a connection sets one weight to zero and the unit stays; deleting a unit removes the whole unit with all its connections; shrinking values makes weights or unit outputs smaller while connections and units remain, and the source also penalizes neuron outputs. A small unit output can still be amplified by large next-layer weights, so check the whole path and the data performance after deleting, and record the three operations separately. On the right is the source's quoted result for a two-layer sigmoid network: under conditions such as a small training error and a weight-norm bound, the complexity term contains A cubed times the square root of log d over N. A is a common bound on each unit's sum of absolute weights, d is the input dimension and N the sample size. With d and N fixed, doubling A makes this term 2 cubed, equal to 8 times (computed by program). This is only the source's order-of-magnitude summary, not a full probability bound, and not a classification error rate. Next, the next page covers cascade correlation.

steps.label: Cascade correlation
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the three operations and the norm. Another route starts from a small architecture: first find a response related to the residual, freeze it, then let the output side lower the error; the two stages must not be mixed into one training objective. The residual is the true target minus the current prediction, and n is the sample index. Cascade correlation adds one hidden unit at a time that responds to the current residual, and the new unit receives the inputs and earlier hidden units: stage one trains the candidate's input weights to maximize the teaching score S; stage two freezes these weights and retrains the output side to lower the squared error. S is the absolute value of the sum of products of the mean-removed candidate output v and residual e, with no division by the standard deviation, so it is not a Pearson coefficient. Take e equal to (−1, 1): the candidate v equal to (−1, 1) gives S equal to 2; the constant candidate v equal to (1, 1) is zero after removing the mean, so S equals 0 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the source's data and settings.

steps.label: Source data and setup
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on cascade correlation. This page keeps the source's report apart from this lecture's calculation. Data: class A has four means (0.4,0.9), (2.0,1.8), (2.3,2.3), (2.6,1.8) and class B has (1.5,1.0), (1.9,1.0), (1.5,3.0), (3.3,2.6); each cluster has 50 points, so 8 times 50 is 400 points; each cluster has covariance 0.08 times the identity, so the standard deviation is the square root of 0.08, about 0.283, not 0.08. The scatter on the left is redrawn from the same setup with the fixed seed 20261025, checks the distribution only, is not the source's original sample, and no network was retrained. The network is 2–3–2–1 with logistic activations, targets 1 and 0, and 9 plus 8 plus 3 equal to 20 parameters with biases. Momentum: μ 0.05 and α 0.85; adaptive momentum: μ 0.01, α 0.85, r_i 1.05, c 1.05 and r_d 0.7. μ is the learning rate, α the momentum coefficient, r_i and r_d the factors that raise and lower the rate, and c the cost-ratio threshold that triggers lowering; this α differs from the regularization weight of the same name. The source reports adaptive momentum is faster in batch mode. Next, the next page covers the pruning report and the supplementary demo.

steps.label: Pruning report and demo
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the source's data and settings. The pruning report is from the source: two hidden layers of 20 units each, a model with 480 weights trained first, saliency checked every 100 epochs, and 25 weights kept at the end. The kept fraction is 25 over 480, about 0.0521, or 5.21%; deleted are 480 minus 25 equal to 455, about 94.79% (computed by program). The source reports improved performance and a boundary going from curved to nearly straight, but this case cannot guarantee that pruning improves generalization everywhere; the source does not state how inputs, outputs and biases were counted, so no unique architecture can be inferred. These experiments were not rerun here. The right side is a supplementary demo, not a training experiment: take the score r equal to x2 minus 0.6 x1 minus 1, the output p equal to 1 over 1 plus e to the minus r, a threshold of 0.5, and draw the p equal to 0.5 contour on a 401 by 401 grid; the farther from the line, the closer p is to 0 or 1. A smooth picture is not an accuracy comparison. Next, the next page covers second-order compensation.

steps.label: Extension: 2nd order
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the pruning report and the supplementary demo. Supplementary quadratic example: the Hessian H has H11 equal to 4, H12 equal to H21 equal to 1 and H22 equal to 2; deleting w1 equal to 0.5 means δw1 equal to minus 0.5. With δw2 equal to 0 the cost is one half times 4 times 0.5 squared, equal to 0.5. Allowing w2 to compensate, ΔJ equals 0.5 minus 0.5 δw2 plus δw2 squared; differentiating in δw2 gives minus 0.5 plus 2 δw2 equal to 0, so δw2 equals 0.25 and the cost is 0.5 minus 0.125 plus 0.0625 equal to 0.4375, below 0.5 (computed by program). When only one weight is deleted and the rest are fixed, the cross term vanishes; letting other weights compensate means the off-diagonal entries must be reconsidered. Bottom right is a numerical check without second derivatives: step a small h along one weight and estimate H_ii by central differences; with J equal to (w minus 0.5) squared, w equal to 0.5 and h equal to 0.1, the three costs are 0.01, 0 and 0.01, giving 2, matching the analytic value. h is the difference step, not the deletion threshold; too large a step gives approximation error and too small may cancel in floating point. Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on second-order compensation. Two exercises. Q1: C has weight 0.5 and curvature 8; D has weight 2 and curvature 0.1; which is deleted first by saliency? s_C equals one half times 8 times 0.5 squared, equal to 1; s_D equals one half times 0.1 times 2 squared, equal to 0.2, so by the estimate D is deleted first; check: a larger weight can have a smaller saliency. Q2: with τ equal to 2 and w equal to 2, compute ρ(w): ρ(2) equals 2 squared over 2 squared plus 2 squared, equal to 4 over 8, equal to 0.5; the weight is still 2, and only zeroing or removing deletes it; check: the penalty is part of the objective, not a deletion (computed by program). That ends this unit; the next KP asks whether many connections can share a few parameters from the start.
